documents.title: AI Appropriate Use Procedure
documents.stance_why: The procedure addresses 'All USU Faculty, Staff & Researchers' and mostly welcomes AI ('USU is forward-looking when it comes to AI'), while listing prohibited uses and data rules. It sets no rule for student coursework and says role-specific syllabus expectations live elsewhere. Overall AI is allowed with conditions, so permit.
documents.summary: USU's appropriate-use procedure for employees sets guiding principles (accountability, verification, disclosure), a three-tier data classification, a list of prohibited uses, and the governance and review of approved AI tools. It is enabling in tone and does not set student coursework rules.

units.why: States the purpose and governing policy of the procedure ("procedure for appropriate AI use as required by Policy 5200"), an institution-level framework preamble, so P56.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. Source: 'This page documents USU's procedure for appropriate AI use as required by Policy 5200, Section 2.8' states the governing policy and purpose of the procedure. Kept as an informs unit (framework statement), P56.
units.anchor: documents USU's procedure for appropriate AI use as required by Policy 5200, Section 2.8

units.why: The page frames the whole procedure as enabling AI use: 'USU is forward-looking when it comes to AI' and asks how to 'enable our people to use these tools'. This is a default welcoming stance, so P02 fits better than P56, which is a framework statement.
units.anchor: USU is forward-looking when it comes to AI

units.why: 'They apply to any AI tool, any workflow, and any role at USU' sets the scope of the guiding principles. That is scope, so P61 fits better than P56 (framework), which would be the type for the stated purpose.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. Source: 'They apply to any AI tool, any workflow, and any role at USU' sets the scope of the principles. B coded P56; the passage defines what the principles cover, which P61 (define AI and the policy's scope) names more directly. Kept, recoded P61.
units.anchor: They apply to any AI tool, any workflow, and any role at USU

units.why: A guiding principle that places responsibility on the user: 'You are accountable for your work product, whether AI helped create it or not.' P29 (own what you submit) fits; the audience is employees but the rule is the same.
units.anchor: You are accountable for your work product, whether AI helped create it or not.

units.why: The principle 'Verify before you trust' says AI output may be 'inaccurate, biased, or incomplete' and must be reviewed. That is the verify-AI-output type P31, not P29, because it is about checking output.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P31/must/during-work; they differed on unit_stance (A neutral, B require). The passage 'Review AI-generated work for accuracy, bias, and copyright compliance before using it' is a condition on AI use that neither requires nor bans using AI, so it takes no position: neutral.
units.anchor: Review AI-generated work for accuracy, bias, and copyright compliance

units.why: 'Before putting any university information into an AI tool, consider its risk classification' is a data-protection duty for users, so P50 (protect personal data); phrased as 'consider', hence should.
units.anchor: Before putting any university information into an AI tool, consider its risk classification.

units.why: Gives a conservative default for data classification ("treat data at the highest applicable tier"), still P50 personal-data protection.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. Source: 'when in doubt, treat data at the highest applicable tier' in 'Know your data' is a conservative default rule; real policy, kept as P50.
units.anchor: when in doubt, treat data at the highest applicable tier

units.why: 'AI supports your judgment; it does not replace it' keeps the human as the decision-maker, matching P32 (stay the primary thinker) rather than P73, since it is general and not about decisions on individuals.
units.resolution_why: A coded modality should, B informs. The source states a principle ('AI supports your judgment; it does not replace it') with no directive verb, under principles described as 'procedural expectations'. It describes the human's role, so informs; P32 kept.
units.anchor: AI supports your judgment; it does not replace it.

units.why: 'Disclose AI use where it is expected or required: in academic work, publications, grant applications, and official communications' is a disclosure duty (P24), conditional on expectations set elsewhere.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P24/must; unit_stance differed (A permit, B require). 'Disclose AI use where it is expected or required' presupposes AI use is allowed and attaches a disclosure condition; it does not require AI use. Final: permit.
units.anchor: Disclose AI use where it is expected or required

units.why: Defers disclosure rules to the journal, funder or department, which P62 names ("deferring to venue, funder" rules).
units.anchor: Follow your department's, journal's, or funding agency's disclosure guidance.
units.fit_note: Also covers department disclosure guidance and academic work, not only research venues. Also defers to the department, not only venue or funder.

units.why: 'Be thoughtful about copyright and licensing when using AI to generate, remix, or repurpose content' is a copyright and licensing consideration (P52); 'thoughtful' makes it should.
units.anchor: Be thoughtful about copyright and licensing when using AI
units.frag_end: regardless of whether AI assisted in the creation.

units.why: Attribution duties stay the same whether or not AI helped ("regardless of whether AI assisted"), so the user owns attribution: P29; P24 would imply an AI disclosure that is not what is said.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. Source: 'Where attribution is expected, provide it, regardless of whether AI assisted in the creation' is an attribution duty distinct from the disclosure sentence before it. Kept as B coded it (P29, the user owns the work product).
units.anchor: Where attribution is expected, provide it

units.why: 'Do not let AI become a source of research misconduct' with fabrication, falsification, plagiarism treated as misconduct: a research-integrity rule, P62 (AI in research and scholarship).
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A general, B when-misuse). 'Do not let AI become a source of research misconduct' with fabrication, falsification and plagiarism defined as misconduct is a principle, not a detection or sanction step. Final: general; P62 (research and scholarship). The two coders' anchors were different parts of the same paragraph, so the units are matched.
units.anchor: Do not let AI become a source of research misconduct.

units.why: 'Before committing to a tool for university work, understand how it handles your data' tells users to research a tool before choosing it: P117 (evaluate a tool), not P65, which is institutional review.
units.anchor: Before committing to a tool for university work, understand how it handles your data.

units.why: Points readers to ai.usu.edu as the "authoritative sources" and says to refer to them: P115 pointer to further guidance.
units.anchor: are the authoritative sources for USU procedures, approved tools

units.why: Tells users to "check back as guidance evolves", a duty to stay current: P102.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. Source: 'check back as guidance evolves alongside the technology' tells users to keep current with the guidance; real instruction, kept as P102 (phase over-time as coded by B).
units.anchor: check back as guidance evolves alongside the technology

units.why: 'Do not acquire a service that USU already provides' is an explicit rule to use centrally provided AI services, i.e. institution-wide licensed tools (P92) rather than a course tool (P17).
units.anchor: Do not acquire a service that USU already provides.

units.why: Moderate-risk data may be used 'only with AI tools that have appropriate institutional or contractual protections', a conditional data rule: P50.
units.anchor: Use only with AI tools that have appropriate institutional or contractual protections in place.

units.why: For high-risk data (FERPA, HIPAA, export-controlled) the text says 'Do not use with consumer AI tools', a data-protection prohibition: P50.
units.anchor: Do not use with consumer AI tools.
units.frag_end: export-controlled data or research data relating to a sponsored project.
units.policy: High-risk data (e.g. FERPA, HIPAA, export-controlled) is not used with consumer AI tools

units.why: 'always classify and treat it at the highest applicable tier' is a rule for data spanning categories; data protection, P50.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. Source: 'When data spans multiple categories, always classify and treat it at the highest applicable tier' is a distinct rule in the data-classification section (B coded the separate 'when in doubt, treat data at the highest applicable tier' in the principles). Real policy; kept as P50 data protection.
units.anchor: always classify and treat it at the highest applicable tier

units.why: Says role-specific guidance, including syllabus expectations, lives on another page, so this document points elsewhere: P115. It sets no syllabus rule itself.
units.anchor: Guidance tailored to faculty, researchers, and administrative staff

units.why: The AI Tools page 'is the source of truth for tool availability and approval status': the university names an approved-tool list to consult, P92.
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A before-course, B general). The sentence names the AI Tools page as 'the source of truth for tool availability and approval status', a reference fact not tied to a time before a course. Final: general.
units.anchor: That page is the source of truth for tool availability and approval status.

units.why: Asks users to judge appropriateness by data, purpose and law, not tool approval alone: weighing context before use, P118.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. Source: 'whether a use of AI is appropriate also depends on the data you put in, what the AI is being used to do or decide, and any law, regulation, or contract that applies' tells users to weigh context beyond tool approval. Real policy, kept as P118 with B's fit_note.
units.anchor: whether a use of AI is appropriate also depends on the data you put in
units.fit_note: Context factors are data, purpose and law, not benefits and values.

units.why: 'Where a service is available through USU's central contracts, that is the approved method of acquisition' requires central procurement of licensed tools: P92.
units.anchor: that is the approved method of acquisition

units.why: 'USU tenant accounts are configured to opt out of contributing your inputs and outputs to AI model training by default' describes a privacy protection of the licensed tools, P50 (prefer vetted tools).
units.resolution_why: Actor differed (A all, B admin). The sentence tells all users what USU tenant accounts do ('opt out of contributing your inputs and outputs... by default'); it is addressed to users of the tools, not to administrators. Final: all.
units.anchor: opt out of contributing your inputs and outputs to AI model training by default

units.why: "always verify that the specific tool you are using is appropriate" is assessing a tool's fit before use, P117.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. Source: 'always verify that the specific tool you are using is appropriate for your data' is a duty to check a tool's fit; real, kept as P117.
units.anchor: always verify that the specific tool you are using is appropriate for your data

units.why: 'Generating content that is illegal under federal or state law, including child sexual abuse material' is a prohibited use: a general conduct ban, P74.
units.anchor: Generating content that is illegal under federal or state law
units.frag_end: prohibited by law or USU policy.

units.why: Prohibited use: creating deepfakes that 'impersonate a real person without their consent' or are 'designed to deceive, harass, defame'. Matches P74 (deceptive or malicious use).
units.anchor: Creating AI-generated images, audio, or video (deepfakes) that realistically impersonate a real person

units.why: Entering export-controlled or CUI data into an unapproved AI tool is prohibited; this is about protecting restricted research data, so P50, not P62.
units.anchor: Entering data subject to export control regulations

units.why: Prohibited use: uploading grant proposals or reviewer materials to AI for peer review; 'NIH and NSF prohibit generative AI in peer review'. Fits P62 (rules for grants and peer review).
units.anchor: Uploading or submitting grant proposals or reviewer materials to any AI tool

units.why: Bans using AI tools operated by entities in listed 'foreign adversary countries' for university work. No type covers a country-based tool ban (P92 is about using approved tools, P65 about review processes), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Using AI tools operated by entities subject to the laws of foreign adversary countries
units.uncovered_note: Bans AI tools operated by entities in named foreign adversary countries for university work. Prohibits use of AI tools operated by entities in listed foreign adversary countries for university work.

units.why: 'Using AI as the sole basis for consequential decisions about individuals, including admissions, financial aid, grades, hiring' is exactly P73 (humans responsible for decisions about people).
units.anchor: Using AI as the sole basis for consequential decisions about individuals

units.why: Prohibits AI use that discriminates on protected bases: 'AI involvement does not change civil-rights obligations'. Compliance with existing law, P77.
units.resolution_why: Type differed (A P77, B UNCOVERED). The source bans 'Any use of AI that would discriminate against individuals on bases protected by Title VI...' and adds 'AI involvement does not change civil-rights obligations'. The passage ties the ban to existing law, which P77 (comply with existing law) covers, so it is not left UNCOVERED; B's point that it also bans a use is recorded in fit_note.
units.anchor: Any use of AI that would discriminate against individuals on bases protected by
units.fit_note: Bans AI uses that discriminate on legally protected bases, grounded in civil-rights law, which goes beyond a general duty to comply with law.

units.why: Prohibits using AI to infer emotional state or sensitive traits of students, employees or applicants. None of the types covers a ban on this kind of inference, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Using AI to infer emotional state, affect, or sensitive traits
units.uncovered_note: Bans using AI to infer emotion or sensitive traits (race, religion, disability, etc.) of students, employees or applicants. Prohibits using AI to infer emotional state or sensitive personal traits of students, employees or applicants.

units.why: 'Using AI to generate content that impersonates another individual in ways intended to deceive' is a ban on deceptive AI use, P74.
units.anchor: Using AI to generate content that impersonates another individual

units.why: 'Using AI tools to probe, exploit, or bypass university security measures' is a ban on malicious AI use that breaches security: P74 (the type lists breaching security).
units.anchor: Using AI tools to probe, exploit, or bypass university security measures

units.why: Prohibits permitting institutional data to 'train or fine-tune external' models, 'regardless of a tool's default settings'. Limits sharing university data with AI providers: P65.
units.resolution_why: Actor differed (A all, B admin). The Prohibited Uses list is introduced as applying 'regardless of which tool is used' and to all users, so the ban on 'Permitting USU institutional data to be used to train... external AI models' binds everyone using AI for USU work. Final: all.
units.anchor: Permitting USU institutional data to be used to train or fine-tune external

units.why: Prohibits processing institutional data in tools USU has not 'procured, evaluated, or approved'; use of approved tools only, P92.
units.anchor: Processing any USU institutional data, regardless of classification, in AI tools

units.why: Names the NIST AI RMF as the institution's framework for AI risk: P56 institution-wide framework.
units.anchor: informed by the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)

units.why: 'Maintains an inventory of approved AI services' describes institutional documentation of deployed AI systems, P98.
units.anchor: is USU's maintained inventory of centrally evaluated AI services

units.why: Names the AI Committee, InfoSec, CDPO and Office of Research as owners of oversight and review: P80.
units.anchor: The USU AI Committee provides executive oversight of AI adoption and this guidance

units.why: 'The AI Tools page and this procedure are reviewed at least annually, and when contracts change or new services are evaluated' sets a review cycle: P54.
units.anchor: reviewed at least annually, and when contracts change or new services are evaluated

units.why: 'Tool approvals are contingent on contracts and configurations remaining in force' and USU may delist a tool: periodic re-evaluation and revocation of approved tools, covered by broadened P65.
units.anchor: Tool approvals are contingent on contracts and configurations remaining in force.

units.why: The governance table says USU 'collects feedback and provides a path to raise concerns' and that 'Individuals affected by an AI-supported decision may raise concerns with the responsible office or the CDPO'. This is a concern path for affected people, which no existing type names (P54 is policy review, P64 is for students accused of misuse), so UNCOVERED; it permits (may) and is addressed to anyone affected.
units.resolution_why: Type, actor, phase and modality differed (A P54 admin over-time informs; B UNCOVERED all when-misuse may). The source: 'Individuals affected by an AI-supported decision may raise concerns with the responsible office or the CDPO.' It is a concern/appeal path for affected people, not a policy-review rule (P54) and not a misuse process for students (P64). A's fit_note (path to raise concerns about AI-supported decisions) and B's uncovered_note say the same thing. Final: UNCOVERED, actor all, phase general (it is not a suspicion/sanction process), modality may.
units.anchor: Individuals affected by an AI-supported decision may raise concerns with the responsible office
units.uncovered_note: People affected by an AI-supported decision may raise concerns with the responsible office or the CDPO (a path to raise concerns and appeal about AI-supported decisions).

units.why: 'USU discourages the use of such services for university work' about foreign-based AI like DeepSeek: discouraged but not forbidden, P03, though the rule concerns tool origin and not learning.
units.anchor: USU discourages the use of such services for university work.
units.fit_note: Concerns foreign-jurisdiction AI services for university work, with a pre-use evaluation expected if necessary.

units.why: Use of a discouraged foreign service requires review with the governing unit first, a prior-approval step: P107.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. Source: for a discouraged foreign AI service, 'you are expected to work with the relevant governing unit to evaluate it before use'. This is a prior-review step distinct from the 'discourages' sentence (matched P03). Kept as P107.
units.anchor: you are expected to work with the relevant governing unit to evaluate it before use

units.why: Departmental website AI chatbots: 'This is a great use of AI, and USU IT is actively working on it.' Welcomes an operational AI use; P76 (administrative and operational AI use).
units.anchor: This is a great use of AI, and USU IT is actively working on it.
units.frag_end: deploy and maintain, without requiring deep technical expertise.

units.why: 'As the person deploying an AI agent, you are accountable for its actions' sets responsibility for autonomous agents: P07 (covers agents), must.
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A general, B during-work). The rule 'As the person deploying an AI agent, you are accountable for its actions' applies at the point of deploying and running an agent, i.e. during work. Final: during-work; P07 with the merged fit_note.
units.anchor: As the person deploying an AI agent, you are accountable for its actions.
units.fit_note: Rule on accountability for deploying agents, not on coding or editor use. Covers agents generally, not editors or IDEs.

units.why: 'ensure agents are properly sandboxed and clearly scoped in what data they can access' is a security control on AI agents: P126.
units.anchor: ensure agents are properly sandboxed and clearly scoped

units.why: 'Any bot you use for university purposes should be sandboxed' with minimum access and no connection to USU data without approval: P126 (access limits on AI agents).
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. Source: 'Any bot you use for university purposes should be sandboxed... minimum access needed' is a separate sentence from 'ensure agents are properly sandboxed' (matched), adding the no-connection-to-USU-data-without-approval condition. Real policy; kept as P126.
units.anchor: Any bot you use for university purposes should be sandboxed

units.why: Warns against giving bots access to email, files or passwords; protecting personal data, P50.
units.resolution_why: Modality differed (A should, B must-not). The source is advice in a section headed 'Your personal data is at stake too': 'If you are not absolutely certain a tool is trustworthy and properly scoped, do not give it access to anything sensitive. When in doubt, give it access to nothing.' It protects the user's own data and carries no sanction, so should-not. The anchor is B's because it carries the actual instruction, and a normalized policy supplies the condition.
units.anchor: do not give it access to anything sensitive
units.policy: If you are not absolutely certain an AI tool or bot is trustworthy and properly scoped, do not give it access to anything sensitive.

units.why: 'Any service that includes AI components should receive additional scrutiny during procurement' with a PIA and security review: institutional review of AI tools before purchase, P65.
units.resolution_why: unit_stance differed (A neutral, B restrict). The sentence sets extra procurement scrutiny, a review step; it does not ban or limit AI use as such. Final: neutral.
units.anchor: Any service that includes AI components should receive additional scrutiny during procurement

units.why: Asks staff to verify vendor protections when a vendor adds AI features: P65 review of vendors.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. Source: 'Do not assume that existing contractual protections automatically extend to AI features added after the original agreement was signed' is a distinct instruction beyond the procurement-scrutiny sentence. Real policy, kept as P65.
units.anchor: Do not assume that existing contractual protections automatically extend to AI features

units.why: Local and self-hosted AI models 'can be a good option for sensitive workflows' and the principles still apply: guidance on protecting data, P50.
units.resolution_why: Phase and modality differed (A general/informs, B during-work/may). 'Local and self-hosted AI models can be a good option for sensitive workflows' is an evaluative statement with no permission or command, so informs; it is not tied to a point in work, so general. unit_stance permit kept because it recommends an option.
units.anchor: Local and self-hosted AI models can be a good option for sensitive workflows
units.frag_end: fit for the purpose you have in mind.

documents.title: AI in Teaching: Communicate about AI
documents.stance_why: The page tells instructors they 'are granted some autonomy to determine their own class guidelines relative to AI' and offers three categories (prohibited, permitted as directed, allowed and encouraged) with templates. It sets no single rule itself, so delegates with the tiers listed.
tiers: AI use permitted as directed with specific assignments
AI use permitted under certain guidelines
documents.summary: Teaching-center guidance telling every instructor to put AI guidelines in the syllabus, with three categories and adaptable template statements for each, advice on assignment-level rules, and modeling responsible AI use. Enforcement goes through Article VI of the Student Code.

units.why: 'every teacher should address the topic of acceptable AI use in their courses' with 'rare exception' is a duty on instructors to address AI, P09.
units.anchor: every teacher should address the topic of acceptable AI use in their courses

units.why: 'teachers should also be able to demonstrate a nuanced understanding of AI technology and how it impacts their discipline' asks instructors to learn AI before setting policy; nearest P63, but P63 is institutional support.
units.anchor: teachers should also be able to demonstrate a nuanced understanding of AI technology
units.fit_note: An expectation on instructors to understand AI, not an offer of workshops or support.

units.why: 'instructors are granted some autonomy to determine their own class guidelines relative to AI' leaves the rule to the instructor: P04, document stance delegates.
units.anchor: instructors are granted some autonomy to determine their own class guidelines relative to AI

units.why: 'such guidelines must be clearly defined in the syllabus' makes the syllabus statement mandatory: P09.
units.anchor: such guidelines must be clearly defined in the syllabus
units.frag_end: Article VI of the student code

units.why: 'enforcement must follow the procedures outlined in Article VI of the student code' requires the formal integrity procedure: P81.
units.anchor: enforcement must follow the procedures outlined in

units.why: 'Class guidelines relative to AI typically fall into three broad categories': prohibited, permitted as directed, allowed and encouraged. Named tiers, P05.
units.anchor: Class guidelines relative to AI typically fall into three broad categories

units.why: Suggests making the category clear to students, a communication practice beyond listing the rule; P66 closest.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. Source: 'Students may find it helpful if they can clearly identify which category a course's AI guidelines fits into' advises instructors to make the category clear to students. A real, if soft, recommendation; kept with B's fit_note.
units.anchor: Students may find it helpful if they can clearly identify which category
units.fit_note: Concerns clarity of category labeling rather than explaining reasons.

units.why: Supplies template statements for instructors to adapt: P110.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. Source: 'Listed below are template guideline statements that may help you draft your own course guidelines' offers templates to instructors. Real policy (P110), kept.
units.anchor: Listed below are template guideline statements that may help you draft your own course guidelines.

units.why: Template for prohibition: 'the use of AI tools to generate content or responses for assignments is prohibited'. Default ban on AI for graded work in that course: P01.
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A during-work, B course-start). The sentence bans using AI 'to generate content or responses for assignments', a rule about doing assignment work, though it is delivered in the syllabus. Final: during-work (what students do), P01.
units.anchor: the use of AI tools to generate content or responses for assignments is prohibited
units.frag_start: In this course, the use of

units.why: The prohibition template lists 'chatbots like ChatGPT and Copilot, image generators, coding assistants', covering built-in assistants: P07 fits partly.
units.resolution_why: Phase and modality differed (A during-work/must-not, B course-start/informs). 'This includes chatbots like ChatGPT and Copilot, image generators, coding assistants' sets which tools the ban covers, so the ban binds them: must-not, during-work. P07 with merged fit_note.
units.anchor: chatbots like ChatGPT and Copilot, image generators, coding assistants
units.fit_note: Lists coding assistants and chatbots as covered by the ban but does not mention editor integration. Lists tool categories covered; does not mention disabling editor features.

units.why: 'Students may not submit work that is wholly or partially generated by AI' bars AI-produced submitted work: P19.
units.anchor: Students may not submit work that is wholly or partially generated by AI.

units.why: Grammar checkers like Grammarly 'should not be used in ways that greatly modify writing style or content': a prose-specific limit, P18.
units.anchor: should not be used in ways that greatly modify writing style or content

units.why: 'An essential outcome of this course is to strengthen students foundational skills' by doing their own work: limiting AI because own work builds skill, P41.
units.resolution_why: Actor and phase differed (A all/general, B student/course-start). The sentence is the template's rationale for students ('An essential outcome of this course is to strengthen students' foundational skills...'). It addresses students in a course, and is a principle rather than an instruction at a point in time. Final: student, general.
units.anchor: foundational skills as thinkers, creators, and communicators by doing and presenting their own work
units.frag_end: with or without the assistance of AI.

units.why: 'assignment submissions may be reviewed by AI detection software such as Copyleaks' allows detector use: P40.
units.anchor: assignment submissions may be reviewed by AI detection software such as Copyleaks

units.why: 'If there is strong suspicion or evidence of AI use in a submission, it may be reported as an academic integrity violation': unauthorized AI as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: it may be reported as an academic integrity violation

units.why: Article 6 'outlines due process for instructors and students, including options for appeal': students have a path to respond, P64.
units.anchor: which outlines due process for instructors and students, including options for appeal

units.why: 'Possible sanctions may include a reduced grade and/or requirement to resubmit the assignment' names penalties in advance: P37.
units.resolution_why: Actor differed (A instructor, B student). 'Possible sanctions may include a reduced grade and/or requirement to resubmit' tells students what consequences they face; the instructor already appears in the detection/reporting units. Final: student.
units.anchor: Possible sanctions may include a reduced grade and/or requirement to resubmit the assignment.

units.why: Template 2: students 'are permitted to use AI tools only for specific assignments and according to specific guidelines'. Whether AI is allowed is decided assignment by assignment, so P04 (not P107, since no closed task list is given).
units.resolution_why: Type and phase differed (A P107 during-work, B P04 course-start). Source: students 'are permitted to use AI tools only for specific assignments and according to specific guidelines'. The text names no closed list of tasks (P107); it makes permission depend on the assignment, which is P04 (decided per assignment). Phase: it governs what students may do in assignment work, so during-work.
units.anchor: permitted to use AI tools only for specific assignments and according to specific guidelines
units.frag_start: In this course, students are permitted

units.why: Guidelines are placed in assignment instructions ("which tools students may use and for what purposes"): P09.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. Source: 'These guidelines are detailed in the assignment instructions and describe which tools students may use and for what purposes' states where the rule lives for the permit-as-directed category. Kept as P09; modality changed from must (B) to informs because the sentence is declarative and gives no command.
units.anchor: These guidelines are detailed in the assignment instructions and describe which tools students may use

units.why: 'For all other assignments and tasks, students are expected to do their own work without the assistance of AI' is the rule for assignments that say nothing: P06.
units.anchor: For all other assignments and tasks, students are expected to do their own work

units.why: 'Students will be responsible for the content and quality of their assignment submissions': ownership of submitted work, P29.
units.anchor: Students will be responsible for the content and quality of their assignment submissions

units.why: Detection applies when AI is "not expressly allowed"; P40. Differs from the first template in scope of use.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this. Source: 'In cases where AI use is not expressly allowed, submissions may be reviewed using AI detection tools' is the second and third templates' detection sentence, which differs from the first template's in scope (only where AI is not allowed). A coded the first template's only; kept as a separate rule.
units.anchor: In cases where AI use is not expressly allowed, submissions may be reviewed using AI

units.why: Template 3: 'students are permitted to use AI tools for all assignments, but only according to specific guidelines' is a permit-with-conditions default. P02 fits partly since the instructor lists the allowed purposes.
units.resolution_why: Phase differed (A during-work, B course-start); B's anchor 'students are permitted to use AI tools' is ambiguous in the text (it also begins the previous template), so the match uses A's anchor, which is unique to template 3. The sentence permits AI for all assignments under guidelines, governing assignment work: during-work. P02 with A's fit_note (permission limited to an instructor-chosen list of purposes).
units.anchor: for all assignments, but only according to specific guidelines
units.frag_start: In this course, students are permitted
units.frag_end: may use AI for the following purposes:
units.fit_note: Permission is limited to an instructor-chosen list of purposes.

units.why: 'Brainstorming ideas' is a listed permitted purpose in the template: P15.
units.anchor: Brainstorming ideas

documents.summary: USU Policy 5200.2.8 sets data-security, accuracy, bias, copyright and accountability expectations for AI use by faculty, staff and students, and points to ai.usu.edu for sample syllabus statements. It encourages responsible use and leaves coursework rules to faculty.

notes: Reconciled from coder A and coder B. Coder A. Doc 1 (appropriate-use procedure) is addressed to faculty, staff and researchers, not students; many units are P50/P62/P74 data and conduct rules. Two UNCOVERED units: ban on AI from foreign-adversary countries, and ban on emotion or sensitive-trait inference. In the teaching page, repeated detector, integrity and sanction sentences in templates 2 and 3 were coded once (template 1). Template text is coded as the policy model offered to instructors, not as a USU rule on students. | Coder B. Duplicate enforcement text repeated across the teach page templates was coded once (first template) plus the 'not expressly allowed' variant. Infosec 2.8 page 'academic' categories are not shown in the saved text. Reconciler: infosec 2.8 'AI in Academic Settings' says USU 'provides the following general categories for AI use in coursework' but the saved text lists none, so that lead-in (coder A only, P05) was dropped; coder A's fit_note on it said it mentions categories but lists none. In the teaching page, template 3 lists 12 purposes; both coders' items are kept (coders A and B each missed some). Topics use the starter codebook codes (coder B's topics; coder A's free-form topics mapped for A-only units).
